title: Economic Outlook and the Labor Market
summary: Fed Vice Chair Philip N. Jefferson delivered a speech at the University of Detroit Mercy on April 7, 2026, outlining his economic outlook. He sees the economy growing at about 2 percent, with inflation remaining above the 2 percent target (PCE at 2.8 percent, core at 3.0 percent as of February), and the labor market roughly in balance with unemployment at 4.3 percent. Jefferson emphasized that progress on disinflation has stalled due to tariff impacts, and that risks exist on both sides of the Fed's dual mandate.
key_points: GDP expanded about 2 percent in 2025; Jefferson expects similar or slightly faster growth in 2026, supported by AI infrastructure investment and deregulation
PCE inflation was 2.8 percent for the 12 months ending February 2026; core PCE was 3.0 percent, with little progress lowering core inflation over the past year
The unemployment rate edged lower to 4.3 percent in March 2026, near estimates of the natural rate, after rising to 4.5 percent in November 2025
Job growth has been uneven: 178,000 jobs added in March, but the 3-month moving average through Q1 2026 was about 70,000 per month, a subdued pace
Labor market is in a 'low-hire, low-fire' state; firms tightened by pausing expansion rather than through widespread layoffs
Inflation progress has stalled mainly due to tariffs; elevated energy prices will add upward pressure to headline inflation in the near term
Trade policy uncertainty and geopolitical tensions (Middle East conflict) pose upside risks to the inflation forecast
why_it_matters: Fed Vice Chair Jefferson's speech provides insight into the current thinking of a senior FOMC voter on the economic outlook and policy path. With inflation remaining above target and the labor market showing signs of stabilization, the speech informs market participants about the Fed's assessment of whether conditions warrant easing or further tightening. His balanced view—acknowledging risks to both sides of the dual mandate—suggests a cautious, data-dependent approach to policy.
macro_context: Jefferson describes an economy growing at potential with labor market roughly in balance, but inflation stuck above target. He explicitly notes that disinflation progress has stalled due to tariffs, and that energy price increases will pressure headline inflation near-term. This suggests the Fed is unlikely to cut rates soon unless inflation shows renewed progress toward 2 percent.
